raw.answer: The case asked how extra pay for overtime work should be calculated under Taiwan's Labor Standards Act. The court said that businesses covered by the Act have had to follow its Article 24 on overtime pay since the Act took effect. The special exemption for monitoring, intermittent and other special-nature work was added only later, so it does not apply to earlier periods.
raw.held: Overtime pay for any industry covered by the Labor Standards Act falls under Article 24 from the time the Act took effect. The later Article 84-1 exemption, added on 27 December 1996, has no application to matters before its effective date.

points.text: The Labor Standards Act sets minimum working conditions to protect workers, and it applies to the industries listed in its Article 3. The Act was later widened so that it was to cover all employment relationships, with exceptions only where truly unworkable.
Businesses may agree other conditions with workers given the nature of the work, but never below the Act's minimum standards. This applies even to monitoring and intermittent work.

Whether work counts as monitoring, intermittent or other special work must be approved and announced by the central authority. Written agreements on working time must be filed with the local authority, so employers and workers cannot decide this alone.
Overtime pay under Article 24 applies to all industries covered by the Act from when the Act took effect.
The exemption from rules on working hours, days off and holidays for special work was added by Article 84-1 and so cannot apply to earlier events.
How working time or rest time is calculated is a factual question decided under the relevant laws for each industry. It is outside this interpretation.

who: Workers in industries covered by the Labor Standards Act

raw.answer: The case asked whether the Chief of the General Staff of the military can be questioned by legislators and may refuse to appear before Legislative Yuan committees. The court decided that legislators cannot question him in the full legislative session under the constitutional provision on ministers, because he is not a head of a ministry. But he is a government official who can be invited to committees, and he generally cannot refuse to appear, though he need not answer questions on important national defense secrets.
raw.held: The Chief of the General Staff is not a ministry head and so is not covered by the legislators' power to question ministers in session. Committees may still invite him to answer questions, and he may refuse only for a proper reason tied to national-security military operations, and need not answer questions involving important defense secrets.

points.text: The Constitution lets legislators question the Premier and ministry heads, as a design based on popular and accountable government. Defense matters can be put to the Premier and the Minister of National Defense.

The Chief of the General Staff is the Defense Minister's chief of staff and answers directly to him, so he is not a ministry head and legislators cannot question him in the full session under that provision.

The Legislative Yuan is the highest legislative body with power over laws, budgets and important state matters. It may set up committees and invite officials to answer questions, so it can understand the matters before it.

Because the Executive Yuan is responsible to the Legislative Yuan, ministry heads and their staff, except those who independently exercise powers free of outside interference, must explain when invited by committees.

The Chief of the General Staff leads military bodies that are not outside the administrative system and handles defense matters including budgets. He is thus a government official who must appear unless there is a proper reason, and questions on important defense secrets need not be answered.

The heads of the Judicial, Examination and Control Yuans may decline invitations out of mutual respect among the five Yuans and constitutional custom. Staff of those Yuans who hold administrative duties must explain matters about their bills and budgets.

who: Heads and staff of the Judicial, Examination and Control Yuans

raw.answer: The case asked whether a rule in the enforcement regulations of the Statute for Upgrading Industries is unconstitutional. The rule gives companies only six months after finishing repayment of equipment loans to apply for a certificate of completion. The court decided the six-month rule is constitutional.
raw.held: The six-month application period in the enforcement rules is in line with the legislative purpose, does not go beyond the parent law, and does not conflict with Articles 19 and 23 of the Constitution.

points.text: Laws cannot spell out every detail, so they may authorize agencies to set technical details by regulation. Such rules are allowed if they fit the legislative purpose and stay within the parent law, judged by the law's purpose and overall provisions rather than just its wording.

The six-month period is short for taxpayers, but the plan already gave a set completion deadline and a possible extension up to four years. Without a fixed application period, the goal of assessing taxes would be hard to achieve.

The period takes account of the real needs of companies covered by the statute, and also of the tax assessment period and the accounting document retention period in other laws. It is therefore necessary to carry out the parent law and related laws.
So the six-month rule fits the legislative purpose, does not exceed the parent law, and does not conflict with Articles 19 and 23.

who: Companies that use retained earnings to increase capital and repay equipment loans
Shareholders receiving the new registered shares
Tax authorities and the agencies that approve repayment plans

raw.answer: The case asked whether the death penalty and life imprisonment set by special drug laws for making, transporting and selling the most serious drugs are unconstitutional. The court decided they are not: the penalties serve a legitimate purpose, are necessary, and do not violate the constitutional protections of life and personal freedom. It also declined to hear parts of the request about possessing drugs with intent to sell and about how courts define 'selling'.
raw.held: The death penalty and life imprisonment provisions in the Eradication of Narcotics Ordinance (Art. 5, para. 1) and the Narcotics Hazard Prevention Act (Art. 4, para. 1) do not violate Article 23 or Article 15 of the Constitution. The requests about the possession-with-intent-to-sell provisions and the court practice on 'selling' were not accepted.

points.text: Protecting life and bodily freedom does not stop the state from setting special criminal penalties, so long as they have a proper purpose, are necessary and are reasonable under Article 23; they cannot be judged only by comparison with ordinary criminal law.
The drug laws aim to wipe out drugs and drug harm, protect public health, keep social order and protect national security, so they target the sources of supply.

Making, transporting and selling drugs are the root of the harm, hurting many people as well as society and the nation, far beyond harm to one individual, so strict special legislation fits the proportionality principle.
Drug harm in the country has lasted a long time and damages families, public strength and generates other crime, so cutting off the source is urgent.
These acts are also very profitable, so long prison terms alone would be unlikely to work and would be unfair; comparing them to murder of an individual is not apt.
The requests on possession with intent to sell were not in the indictment and not shown to be applicable law, and the meaning of 'selling' is a matter of interpretation, so they were not accepted.

who: People accused of making, transporting or selling first-level drugs

raw.answer: The case asked whether banking and credit cooperative rules are unconstitutional because they do not set out procedures for the authorities' actions against financial institutions, such as taking them over. The court found the rules do not fully match the constitutional protection of property rights. It ordered the responsible authorities to review and amend them promptly.
raw.held: The banking law, the credit cooperative law and the financial institution supervision and takeover measures do not fully fit the constitution's protection of property rights, and the authorities must review and revise them as soon as possible in line with this ruling.

points.text: The constitution protects property rights. Limits on them must be necessary and set by law, and orders issued under a delegation must follow the legislature's purpose and stay within the authority granted.

The laws exist to protect depositors and keep the financial order stable, and the takeover measures have a legal basis in the banking law. Even so, laws must also provide reasonable procedures and timely court remedies, and orders must set necessary procedures for actions affecting people's rights.

The measures seriously affect shareholders, members, managers and other interested parties. Yet the rules only provide for the authority issuing administrative decisions and do not say when it must hear their views or consult local government bodies first.

The takeover measures let the authority appoint supervisors or takeover persons, give them management and disposal powers, and decide on transferring business, assets and liabilities or on mergers. This does not require considering whether a shareholders' or members' meeting could decide, or whether the institution could supply funds, security or other means to cover its debts.
The court also suggested a broad review of financial management to prevent crises, and said the management of credit cooperatives should respect the constitutional aim of encouraging cooperatives.

who: Shareholders and members of banks and credit cooperatives
Financial regulators and local government bodies

raw.answer: The case asked whether a Ministry of Economic Affairs circular was unconstitutional for treating a company's dissolution or cancelled registration as 'ceasing business', which made its trademark rights end automatically. The court held that the circular went beyond what the Trademark Act allowed and conflicted with the constitutional protection of property, so it should no longer be applied.
raw.held: The part of the 1985 Ministry of Economic Affairs circular that treats a company's dissolution or cancelled registration as 'ceasing business' goes too far, conflicts with the constitutional protection of property, and is not to be applied.

points.text: The Constitution protects property, and trademark rights are a kind of property.

A trademark right ends automatically only when the owner has stopped business and there is no possibility of licensing it or transferring it to someone who continues the business, because then it has lost its purpose.
A temporary pause in business, or an owner ending business while a transfer to someone else remains possible, is not the same as ceasing business, since the trademark still has value in use.
A dissolved company is treated as not yet dissolved within the scope of liquidation, and may temporarily carry on business to wind up affairs and ease liquidation.

A dissolved company that is still operating its original business cannot be said to have ceased business, so its trademark right is not automatically extinguished, and it may transfer the trademark with its business.

By equating dissolution or cancelled registration with ceasing business, the circular ignored the civil and company law rules and wrongly ended trademark rights that still had value, exceeding the limit set by the Trademark Act.

who: Businesses buying a company's business and trademark

raw.answer: The case asked whether an earlier Judicial Yuan interpretation (No. 1850), which barred conscripts from filing administrative appeals against military service grade decisions, was unconstitutional. The court held that a decision on a man's service grade is an administrative act he can challenge through appeal and court action. It said the earlier interpretation no longer applies.
raw.held: A military service grade decision is an administrative disposition, so the man concerned may file an administrative appeal and administrative lawsuit if he thinks it unlawful or improper. Interpretation No. 1850 is no longer to be applied, and Article 69 of the Enforcement Act of the Military Service Act does not conflict with the Constitution.

points.text: Article 16 of the Constitution protects the right to file administrative appeals and lawsuits, so people can get final relief from public authority and agencies can correct unlawful or improper acts.

A one-sided act by an agency that takes direct legal effect outward counts as an administrative disposition regardless of its wording or form. Treating such an act as not a disposition conflicts with the constitutional right, as Interpretation No. 423 already said.

Under Article 34 of the Military Service Act, men are sorted into five grades that decide whether and what kind of service they perform. This decision directly affects their constitutional rights, so it is an administrative disposition.
Because it is an administrative disposition, a conscript who thinks the decision unlawful or improper may file an administrative appeal and lawsuit.

Interpretation No. 1850 limited remedies to a special petition to a superior conscription officer and barred ordinary appeals. This is inconsistent with the above and with the constitutional protection of the right to sue, so it is no longer applied.

Article 69 of the Enforcement Act only requires exemption, prohibition, deferment and postponement to be approved and reviewed first by the authority. It does not limit the right to dispute, and those unhappy with the review result may still appeal and sue.

who: Those given exemption or deferment decisions

raw.answer: Some members of the Legislative Yuan asked the Constitutional Court whether the constitutional amendments of September 1999 were unconstitutional. The court agreed to hear the case and found the amendments defective: the National Assembly passed them by secret ballot, picked its members in a way that did not involve an election, and extended its own term and the legislators' terms without proper reason. It declared the amended Articles 1, 4, 9 and 10 void from the date of the ruling, and the earlier 1997 amendments continue to apply.
raw.held: The 1999 amendments to Articles 1, 4, 9 and 10 lose effect from the day the ruling is published, and the amendments published on 21 July 1997 continue to apply.

points.text: The court said it has the power to hear the case, because the constitution gives it authority over questions about how the constitution is enforced and amended. It rejected the National Assembly's objections, including that internal procedure is outside court review.

Amending the constitution directly expresses the people's sovereignty, so it must be open and transparent. Passing the amendments by secret ballot violated that principle and the Assembly's own rule on voting. A third or more of those present had asked for a recorded vote.

The defect was clear and serious enough to deprive the amendment of its effect. The facts could be seen from the record without investigation, and the people could not tell how representatives voted or hold them accountable.

Basic principles such as the democratic republic, popular sovereignty, protection of rights, and separation and balance of powers cannot be changed by an amendment without destroying the constitutional order.

Assembly members were to be allocated from the results of the legislative elections, so they would be party appointees rather than elected. This conflicts with Article 25 and the democratic principle.

Extending the terms of Assembly members and legislators had no justification such as a grave national crisis that made elections impossible. The Assembly's self-extension also breached the principle of avoiding conflicts of interest.

raw.answer: The case asked whether a government personnel agency's 1974 interpretation was unconstitutional. It said staff who took unpaid leave to enter military service had their years of service recognized after returning to their posts. The court found that this left out military service done before becoming a civil servant, which did not match the equality principle, and it gave the authorities one year to fix the rules.
raw.held: The agency's interpretation does not match the ruling's meaning, because it lets conscripts count military service toward civil-servant retirement years only if they served after becoming civil servants. The relevant authorities must, within one year of the ruling, set proper rules by law or through the Executive Yuan together with the Examination Yuan.

points.text: The state must provide civil servants with pay and retirement benefits to support their livelihood, and soldiers are a kind of civil servant. They may receive discharge or retirement pay, or combine military years with civil-service years for retirement.
Counting military service does not depend on whether it was voluntary or conscripted, or on whether it came before or after becoming a civil servant.

Under Article 20 of the Constitution, people have a duty to serve in the military as the law provides. Conscripts owe the same loyalty and perform the same duties as volunteers, even if their service length and expertise differ, so their rights to count service years should not differ.

The Act on Preferential Treatment of Soldiers and Their Families, Article 32, paragraph 1, requires reserve soldiers' military years to be counted when they move into public office. It makes no distinction between voluntary and conscripted service, and rests on the constitutional equality principle.

The 1974 interpretation allowed conscripts to combine service only if it came after they became civil servants, and refused to count conscript service before that. This conflicts with the equality principle.
Counting this service greatly affects civil servants' rights and should be protected, so the court ordered the authorities to set rules within one year.

who: Conscripted soldiers who later became civil servants
Volunteer soldiers who became civil servants
Civil servants who entered service on unpaid leave
Government authorities that must set the rules

raw.answer: The case asked whether the presidential and vice-presidential election law's rules on collecting signatures and paying a deposit to run for office are unconstitutional. The court decided they are not: the signature threshold and the NT$1 million deposit stay within what the legislature may decide. It added that these requirements should be reviewed and improved over time as society and politics change.
raw.held: The signature requirement (1.5% of the voters in the latest central representative election) and the NT$1 million deposit do not violate the Constitution, and neither does the implementing rule that lets the Central Election Commission refuse incomplete or underfunded applications. The requirements should be reviewed from time to time.

points.text: The Constitution lets the legislature set presidential election procedures by law, and they must be fair and reasonable. Rules that do not go beyond what is necessary do not violate voting rights or the right to stand for election.

The signature requirement shows a candidate has real political support, balances the rules for party-nominated candidates, and discourages casual candidacies that waste public resources. It is a reasonable rule, not an unnecessary limit on the right to stand, and does not breach equality.
The signature count was workable in practice: in the ninth election, over 1.05 million signature documents were checked one by one by election commissions.

The NT$1 million deposit ensures at least half the required signatures are gathered, and it is returned once that number is reached. It does not force candidates to bear huge election costs, so it stays within the legislature's discretion.

The implementing rules were made under a law that clearly states their purpose and scope. Rejecting incomplete, non-compliant or underfunded applications fits that authorization and does not conflict with the Constitution.
The conditions for exercising the right to stand should be reviewed and improved over time as society and politics change, to serve the Constitution's protection of political participation.

who: Would-be presidential and vice-presidential candidates running by signature
Central Election Commission and local election commissions

raw.answer: The case asked whether a rule in the Labor Insurance Act's enforcement rules, which let only full-time employees join labor insurance, was unconstitutional. The court found that the rule added a limit the Act itself does not have and failed to protect non-full-time workers who qualify under the Act. It held the rule should not be applied.
raw.held: Article 25, paragraph 1 of the enforcement rules, as it stood before the 13 September 1996 amendment, limited insured status to full-time employees. It went beyond what the law allowed and conflicts with the spirit of Article 23 of the Constitution, so it should not be applied.

points.text: The Constitution requires the state to protect labor, and the Labor Insurance Act was made to secure workers' livelihoods and promote social security.

Limits on people's rights must be set by law and go no further than necessary. Enforcement rules may only cover details and technical matters, and may not contradict the parent law or add limits the law does not have.

The Act does not restrict insured status to full-time employees, and a worker's status as a worker is the same whether the work is temporary, short-term, seasonal, specific or continuing. Who may be insured affects workers' rights, so it must be set by law.
The enforcement rule excluded part-time and other non-full-time workers. Its aim was to stop people who are not workers from being enrolled falsely to claim benefits and drain insurance funds.
Even so, the rule ignored the interests of non-full-time workers who meet the Act's requirements, which conflicts with the aim of protecting workers.
By limiting who could be insured beyond what the Act says, the rule exceeded the necessary scope of its legal authorization and does not fit Article 23, so it should not be applied.

who: Non-full-time or part-time employees and workers
Employees and workers covered by the Labor Insurance Act
Employers and units that enroll workers in insurance

raw.answer: The case asked whether officials of local governments must appear before committees of the Legislative Yuan (the national legislature) when invited to answer questions. The court decided that, unless a law expressly requires it, they are not obliged to appear and may decide for themselves whether attending to explain is necessary. The Legislative Yuan also may not cut or hold up central government subsidy budgets for local governments just because their officials did not appear.
raw.held: Local government executive officials, unless a law expressly says they must attend, may weigh the need to explain and decide whether to appear at Legislative Yuan committees. If they do not appear, the Legislative Yuan may not use that as a reason to cut or shelve central subsidy budgets for the local government.

points.text: Local self-government is a system protected by the Constitution, so local governments can run their own affairs and share power with the central government in a cooperative, vertically divided arrangement.

Local governments have their own elected executive and legislative bodies, with checks between them. Higher governments may only supervise lawfulness or appropriateness, so local governments hold an independent position that state organs must respect.

Central government officials must answer to the Legislative Yuan when invited under Article 67, paragraph 2 of the Constitution (as held in Interpretation No. 461). But given the separation of powers and the balanced division of central and local powers, local officials need separate rules.

Because local self-government has its own autonomy and both levels have their own legislatures, local officials do not have to appear unless a law expressly requires it. They may decide whether attending is necessary.
The central government may give local governments suitable subsidies depending on their finances, so that local governments can meet basic needs and the nation can develop in a balanced way.

So the Legislative Yuan may not cut or hold back such subsidy budgets because local officials did not attend, in order to keep local self-government working and respect the constitutional balance of central and local powers.

who: Central government agencies that grant subsidies

raw.answer: The case asked whether a provision of the law on relations between the Taiwan area and the mainland is unconstitutional because it leaves certain government bonds issued on the mainland unaddressed. The court decided it is not unconstitutional. It reasoned that the bonds' backing has changed, that immediate repayment would burden Taiwan-area taxpayers unfairly, and that delaying repayment until national unification is authorized and necessary.
raw.held: Article 63, paragraph 3 of the Act, which leaves certain pre-1949 mainland bonds and pre-withdrawal debts of state banks and deposit-taking institutions unaddressed until national unification, delays creditors' claims against the state. This is consistent with the constitutional amendment and does not conflict with Article 23 or the Constitution.

points.text: The Additional Articles of the Constitution, Article 11, allow special legislation on rights, obligations and other affairs between the free area and the mainland area.
The pre-1949 mainland bonds were backed by mainland tax revenue and state assets, and the amounts were very large. After the government moved to Taiwan, that backing changed.
Immediate repayment by the government would put a heavy tax burden on people in the Taiwan area, which would clearly violate the principle of fairness.

Individual freedoms and rights may be limited by law for the public interest if the conditions of Article 23 are met. Where the Constitution clearly authorizes special legislation, a law within those conditions does not conflict with it.

The Act was made under the authority of Article 11 of the Additional Articles. Postponing these debts until unification delays creditors' claims. The court called this a necessary measure given changed circumstances and the national situation, so it does not conflict with the Constitution.

who: Creditors of state banks and deposit institutions from before their withdrawal from the mainland

raw.answer: The case was about a Ministry of Finance letter that said people who sell their owner-occupied home land and buy new land within two years could only get a land value increment tax refund if the tax office had approved the lower owner-occupied residential rate for their land tax. The court decided that this extra requirement is not found in the Land Tax Act and is unconstitutional, so it can no longer be applied.
raw.held: The part of the Ministry of Finance letter requiring prior tax office approval of the owner-occupied residential land tax rate as a condition for a refund adds a restriction the law does not contain. It violates the principle that taxes must be set by law (Constitution Article 19) and is not to be applied.

points.text: The Land Tax Act sets the legal conditions under which a taxpayer may apply for a refund of land value increment tax after selling owner-occupied residential land and buying new land.

Under the Act, owner-occupied residential land means land where the owner, spouse or direct relatives have registered their household, with no renting out or business use. It does not require tax office approval of the lower land tax rate.
Applying for the lower owner-occupied rate on land tax is a right the owner may choose to use, so not applying cannot by itself be taken to mean the land was rented out or used for business.

Approval of the lower rate can serve as a reference for the tax office. If doubts arise, the office must still check actual renting or business use, and the owner may prove the land was used as a home.
Making approval a refund requirement adds a restriction the Act does not contain, violating Article 19's principle that taxes be set by law, so that part is not to be applied.
Whether the underlying case meets the refund requirements is still for the authorities to judge on all relevant materials and evidence.

who: Owners who sold owner-occupied residential land and bought new land

raw.answer: The case asked whether a past court precedent barring civil servants from filing administrative appeals against disciplinary actions was unconstitutional, and how university teacher promotion reviews should work. The court decided that decisions on teacher promotions by university review committees and the Ministry of Education's final approval are administrative dispositions that teachers can challenge in administrative court after exhausting administrative remedies. It also set requirements for fair, expert-based review procedures and said the conflicting part of the precedent no longer applies.
raw.held: University review committees' promotion decisions and the Ministry of Education's academic review committee's final approval are administrative dispositions, so dissatisfied teachers may sue in administrative court after exhausting administrative remedies. The conflicting part of Administrative Court precedent No. 398 (1962) is no longer to be applied, and the promotion review rules must be comprehensively reviewed and revised.

points.text: People's right to file administrative appeals and lawsuits is protected by the Constitution and is not lost because of a person's status; unilateral acts by bodies exercising delegated public power are administrative dispositions regardless of wording or form.

Under the cited laws, university review committees review promotions and the Ministry of Education approves teacher qualifications, so this is public power exercised under legal authorization that seriously affects teachers' status and rights, making it an administrative disposition open to court challenge.
Because the old precedent barred appeals by those with a civil servant status, the part inconsistent with this reading no longer applies.

Promotion review affects teacher quality, teaching and research standards, and people's right to work and professional qualifications, so procedures must be legally based and ensure objective, fair and accurate assessment, in line with the proportionality principle.

Because review protects academic quality, decisions must rest on objective expertise, so qualified experts in the field should review first and the review committee should respect their judgment unless it gives specific, professionally grounded reasons.
Appeal bodies and administrative courts may check whether procedures were followed and whether judgments were unlawful or clearly inappropriate; the current rules must be revised in light of this.

who: University and college teachers seeking promotion

raw.answer: The case asked which court should hear disputes over civil servant insurance payments. The court said these disputes are public-law matters that must go through administrative appeal procedures. Because those procedures can't always make the payment actually happen, people may go to an ordinary court if the administrative route fails to deliver the payment.
raw.held: Disputes over civil servant insurance benefits must be resolved through administrative procedures. Until the law is reformed, if that route cannot actually produce the payment, the person may sue in an ordinary court.

points.text: The constitutional right to bring a lawsuit ensures people can sue through lawful procedures and get a fair trial. Whether the route is ordinary or administrative court is for the legislature to design.
Taiwan uses two separate court systems: ordinary courts hear private-law disputes and administrative courts hear public-law disputes, unless a law says otherwise.
No law says which court hears civil servant insurance disputes, so the route depends on the nature of the case and what the existing litigation system can do.

Civil servant insurance is a form of social insurance with a public-law nature, so disputes should go through administrative appeal procedures, as earlier interpretations Nos. 266 and 312 also explained.
Administrative litigation currently has no kind of suit besides damages attached to a case, so winning an administrative case does not necessarily mean the person receives the payment.

Until the system is fully revised, people need an effective remedy, so if administrative relief cannot deliver the payment they may sue in an ordinary court. The responsible authorities should quickly complete the revision.

who: Civil servants' beneficiaries claiming insurance payments
Authorities responsible for reforming administrative litigation

raw.answer: The case asked whether the Council of Agriculture's 1989 public notice listing the elephant family as an endangered protected species was unconstitutional. The court decided the listing, and the law's punishment of illegal trade in listed animals and their products, do not violate the Constitution. It added that people who lawfully imported such animals or products before the listing now face limits on their property rights, and the authorities should review the rules and provide reasonable relief.
raw.held: The listing of the elephant family as endangered, and the penalty for illegal trade in listed animals and products, are not unconstitutional. The relevant agencies must review and revise the rules to give reasonable relief to those whose property rights were limited by pre-listing lawful imports.

points.text: The notice was issued under authority given by the Wildlife Conservation Act, and the Act itself clearly set out the content and scope of that authority, so it did not breach the principle of clear authorization.

Trade in endangered animals and their products needs government permission, so unpermitted trade is illegal trade in the listed controlled animals and products, and punishing it is needed to protect endangered and rare wildlife.
Only acts done after the listing are punished, so the penalty does not retroactively harm personal liberty or property rights.

These measures make up for past shortfalls in protecting the environment, are a necessary means to the goal of protecting the environment and ecology, fit the proportionality principle, and serve the public interest.

For animals and products lawfully imported before the listing, the ban on selling, exchanging or displaying for sale limits property rights, so the agencies should look at how severe the limit is and revise the rules to give reasonable relief.

who: Traders in listed wildlife and their products
People who lawfully imported such animals or products before the listing
Government agencies responsible for wildlife protection

raw.answer: The case asked whether a Supreme Court precedent was unconstitutional because it limited when people can claim state compensation for officials who fail to do their duty. The court held that the precedent, to the extent it requires the injured person to have a public-law right to demand the official act and to have asked for it, adds a limit the law does not contain. That part conflicts with the constitution's protection of people's rights and should no longer be applied.
raw.held: When a law aims to protect life, body or property, clearly sets out the duty, and leaves an official no discretion to refrain, an official's negligent failure to act lets the injured specific person seek state compensation. The precedent's inconsistent parts are unconstitutional and must not be applied.

points.text: Article 24 of the Constitution sets out the state's duty to compensate in principle, and where the legal conditions for state liability are met, courts should not read the law narrowly so that people cannot exercise their rights.

Under the State Compensation Act Article 2(2), liability arises when an official's conduct meets the listed conditions (exercise of public power, intent or negligence, unlawfulness, causation) and is not caused purely by natural disaster or force majeure. It does not require that the victim had a public-law right to demand the act and asked for it.

Laws differ in purpose. Where a law only grants authority or leaves discretion, an official's inaction may not directly harm rights or may be a mere question of administrative judgment, so there is no state compensation.
Where a law protects life, body or property, clearly sets the duty, and leaves no room to refrain, negligent or refused performance that harms a specific person entitles the victim to compensation.

Whether a law protects specific individuals is decided case by case. It does if the law grants rights or claims to identifiable people, or if its overall structure, scope, intended effects and social factors show it also protects specific persons.

The precedent still applies where there is a public-law claim and a lawful request, but its inconsistent parts add a limit the law does not contain and violate constitutional protection of rights, so they are not to be applied.

who: People harmed by officials' failure to perform their duties
Public officials and the agencies responsible for their duties
Courts applying the State Compensation Act

raw.answer: The case asked whether a rule in the firearms control law was unconstitutional. The rule required anyone convicted of certain offenses and sentenced to prison to be sent to forced labor for three years after serving the sentence. The court decided that the blanket rule goes too far, because it applies even to people who pose no danger to society.
raw.held: The part of Article 19(1) of the Firearms, Ammunition and Knives Control Act that automatically orders three years of forced labor, whether or not it is needed to prevent or correct a person's danger to society, violates the proportionality principle in Article 23 of the Constitution. That part may not be applied from the day the interpretation was announced.

points.text: Personal freedom is protected by Article 8 of the Constitution. Any law limiting it must meet the requirements of Article 23, and the punishment must reasonably fit its goal.

Security measures such as forced labor are meant to educate and treat a person because of their future danger. They supplement criminal punishment but also restrict bodily freedom much as punishment does, so they must be proportionate.
Proportionality means the measure must fit how serious the act was, how dangerous the person has shown themselves to be, and what can be expected of their future conduct.

Forced labor aims to have offenders learn a skill and a proper attitude to earning a living so they can return to society. Under the Criminal Code and the theft-offender law, courts decide case by case according to the person's dangerousness.
The firearms provision imposes three years of forced labor on everyone convicted, even those with no social danger. This is out of proportion to its goal of prevention and correction.

Where a case fits proportionality, the firearms law still applies. Where it does not, but a security measure is still needed, the court decides under Article 90(1) of the Criminal Code, and the more favorable rule applies.

who: People convicted under the listed firearms offenses and sentenced to prison
People who pose no danger to society and would be sent to forced labor
Authorities responsible for revising the law

raw.answer: The case asked whether the Fujian Provincial Government Organization Rules were unconstitutional because they do not provide for an elected provincial governor and elected provincial assembly members. The court decided they were not unconstitutional. It found the rules reasonably reflect Fujian's special circumstances and fit the authority given by the parent law.
raw.held: The Fujian Provincial Government Organization Rules, which do not provide for popular election of the governor or assembly members, are a necessary response to Fujian's special situation, match what the parent law authorized, and do not violate the constitutional principle of equality before the law (Article 7).

points.text: The constitutional amendment's rules on an elected governor and assembly apply to provinces that can in fact practice self-government, and those rules are set by law rather than being bound by the related constitutional articles.

The Provincial and County Self-Government Act, made under constitutional authority, let the Executive Yuan set the organization of provinces with incomplete territory, because there was no need to apply provincial self-government there.
The Fujian rules (a committee of seven to eleven members, one as chairman, appointed on the Premier's nomination, with no provincial assembly) fit Fujian's special facts and the parent law's purpose.

The Constitution provides for county self-government itself but leaves provincial self-government to law, and the equality principle allows reasonable different rules for different factual situations.

Fujian's area and population are far smaller than before and its public affairs are much lighter than Taiwan Province's, so a leaner organization is suitable, making the rules a reasonable difference that does not breach equality.
Even after the 1997 amendments and the repeal of the self-government act, provinces with special territory may still have their provincial organization adjusted differently under this interpretation.

raw.answer: The case asked whether a Ministry of Finance directive was unconstitutional. The directive let tax offices hold back deed tax bills when several people applied to pay deed tax on the same building or land. The court held that the directive went beyond the statute, blocked people from completing the tax steps needed to register ownership, and conflicted with the constitutional protection of property, so it should no longer be applied.
raw.held: The Ministry of Finance's 1981 directive allowing tax offices to delay issuing deed tax notices until the parties agree or a court rules is inconsistent with Article 15 of the Constitution (protection of property) and may no longer be applied.

points.text: Under the Deed Tax Act, paying deed tax is tied to exercising and acquiring property rights, because land offices register a change of ownership only on a deed tax payment receipt.
When several people apply in turn for the same building or land, the tax office must promptly issue a tax notice to each applicant so they can pay and then register the change.
Civil disputes should be resolved by the parties through legal procedures, and administrative agencies should not step in and require them to negotiate an agreement.

Where one item is sold to several buyers, each contract is valid. Under the principle of equal claims, no buyer's claim excludes the others, and each may request registration of the ownership transfer.

The directive went beyond the statute by letting offices delay the notices. People could not finish the tax steps needed to register ownership, which harmed their exercise of property rights and conflicts with Article 15.

who: People applying to pay deed tax on property

raw.answer: The case asked whether Article 31-1 of the Customs Anti-Smuggling Act is unconstitutional. That article confiscates imported or transshipped cargo when it does not match the manifest, cargo list, transshipment list or shipping contract documents. The court held that it does not conflict with Article 23 of the Constitution.
raw.held: Article 31-1 of the Customs Anti-Smuggling Act, which confiscates goods that do not match the shipping documents unless they were proven to be loaded by mistake, is not in conflict with Article 23 of the Constitution.

points.text: Customs is responsible for catching smuggling, defined as moving goods across the border without declaring them in order to evade inspection, duties or controls.
How customs should inspect and what measures it uses to stop smuggling is for the legislature to decide, based on trade practice, customs work and enforcement methods.

Under Interpretation No. 275, a person who breaks a legal duty need not have acted intentionally but must be at fault. Where the act only breaks a prohibition or duty, fault is presumed unless the person proves otherwise.
In normal international trade, exporters must give correct documents to carriers, and importers should require that the contracted goods be shipped, to avoid mismatches that break import law.
So the article requires importers and exporters to follow standard trade and shipping procedures and record and declare goods honestly in the documents.
Those who can prove a mistaken loading avoid confiscation, the rule does not displace Interpretation No. 275, and it is necessary for the public interest.

raw.answer: The case asked whether, after the 1997 constitutional amendments took effect, Taiwan's provinces are still legal public bodies (public juridical persons). The court decided that provinces remain a level of local government but are no longer local self-governing bodies. They can still be public juridical persons in a limited way, for matters that laws assign to the province and that are not assigned to the nation or to counties and cities.
raw.held: Under Article 9 of the amended Constitution, a province remains a level of local government but has no self-governing matters set by the Constitution and no power to organize itself, so it is not a self-governing public body. A province may still have public-body status to the extent that laws passed consistently with the amendments leave matters within its authority and let it hold rights and duties.

points.text: The court said it was interpreting how the Constitution applies, not reviewing whether a law is unconstitutional.
To be a self-governing public body, a regional body must have power to make and carry out rules on its own self-governing matters and must have the power to organize itself.

Under Article 9 of the amendments, the province stays a level of local government. But since 21 December 1998 it has had no constitutionally set self-governing matters and no power to organize itself, so it is not a self-governing public body.

Other public bodies can exist besides the nation and self-governing bodies, such as bodies with compulsory membership that exercise public power and can hold rights and duties. Existing law already recognizes such bodies.

Article 9 authorizes the legislature to set by law the province's organization, powers and relations. So a law consistent with the amendments can leave matters to the province, and to that extent the province can be another kind of public body.

The authority in Article 9, paragraph 3 to adjust the Taiwan Provincial Government's functions by special law does not let the legislature ignore the limits the amendments set on how the provincial government is organized.

who: The legislature that makes laws on provinces

raw.answer: The case asked whether a regulation under the Civil Servants Insurance Act, which set a time limit for claiming insurance payouts, was unconstitutional. The court held that such a time limit must be set by law, not by an administrative regulation, so the regulation's time limit cannot be applied. Until a law sets one, similar time limits in other civil servant laws are to be applied by analogy.
raw.held: The regulation that directly set the time limit for claiming insurance payouts does not fit the constitution's requirement that this be set by law and must not be applied. Until a law is made, the time limits for retirement or pension claims apply by analogy, and the Civil Code rules apply by analogy for interruption and suspension of the limit.

points.text: Limits on people's rights must be set by law and not go beyond what is necessary; matters that require a law cannot be set by regulation. Implementing rules made under a law's authority must not exceed the parent law or add restrictions it lacks.
The insurance act provides cash payments for disability, old age, death and family funeral events but sets no time limit for claims, so the authority set one in its implementing rules.

A limitation period matters greatly to people's rights and duties, protects existing situations, keeps legal order stable and serves the public interest, so it must be set directly by law and not left to administrative regulation.

The old rule (two years, later changed to five) therefore does not fit this requirement and is not to be applied; meanwhile retirement and pension claim time limits apply by analogy, and Civil Code provisions apply by analogy for interruption and suspension.

who: Civil servants' families claiming insurance payouts
The examination and administrative authorities that make implementing rules

raw.answer: The case asked whether two Ministry of the Interior rules on mainland Chinese people entering Taiwan, covering who qualifies, the approval process and how long they may stay, were unconstitutional. The court decided they were not. It found the rules fit the law that authorized them and do not conflict with the Constitution.
raw.held: The two Ministry of the Interior permit rules setting entry qualifications, approval procedures and stay periods for mainland Chinese people do not go beyond what the parent law allows. They are necessary to maintain social order or advance the public interest, and they do not violate the constitutional amendment or Article 23 of the Constitution.

points.text: Freedom of residence and movement is protected by the Constitution, but it may be limited by law when necessary to prevent harm to others, avoid emergencies, maintain social order or advance the public interest (Article 23).

The constitutional amendment allows special legislation on the rights and duties between the Free Area and the mainland area. The 1992 Act on relations between the two areas was made under it, as special legislation to protect Taiwan's security and people's well-being before national unification.

When a law authorizes regulations that limit people's freedoms, the authorization must be specific. If it is only a general authorization, its meaning is read from the law as a whole, not from the wording of one provision (citing Interpretation No. 394).

The Ministry issued the two permit rules under the Act's articles 10 and 17, and under article 18 which lets authorities deport those who overstay. The rules set entry qualifications, approval procedures, stay periods and penalties for overstaying.
The rules match the Act's purpose, stay within the authority it gave, and are necessary for social order or the public interest. So they do not conflict with the amendment or Article 23.

who: Mainland Chinese people seeking to enter Taiwan
Mainland Chinese people seeking to settle or stay in Taiwan
Ministry of the Interior and security authorities

raw.answer: The case asked whether a rule in the Wrongful Imprisonment Compensation Act is constitutional. The rule denied compensation to people who were detained but then not prosecuted or found not guilty, if their conduct violated public order or good morals. The court found the rule does not fully fit the constitution's proportionality principle and ordered that the conflicting part not be applied.
raw.held: Article 2, item 2, first part of the Act, to the extent it conflicts with this ruling, is not to be applied. It denies compensation based only on a violation of public order or good morals, without considering how serious the conduct was or whether it went beyond what society commonly tolerates.

points.text: The Wrongful Imprisonment Compensation Act is a special law on state liability. Under Article 24 of the Constitution, the legislature must make state compensation laws, and the conditions they set for claims must meet the proportionality principle.

Detaining a criminal defendant seriously restricts personal freedom before a final guilty verdict, so compensation for detention must especially respect the constitution's protection of personal liberty.

The rule aims to protect social order and public morals, but it bars compensation merely because public order or good morals were violated, without asking whether the conduct was serious enough to be intolerable to society's common view.
Compared with the other grounds for denial in the same item and article, this ground is out of balance, so it does not fully fit the proportionality principle.
The Review Committee's decisions are treated as equal to final court judgments, so people may ask for a constitutional interpretation of the laws those decisions applied.

who: People detained but then not prosecuted or acquitted

raw.answer: The case asked whether the Civil Servant Evaluation Act let a government agency's rule decide when a civil servant is fired, since the Act left the standard for 'two major demerits in one evaluation' to the Ministry of Civil Service. The court found this inconsistent with the Constitution because dismissal restricts the right to hold public office and its conditions must be set by law. It also set out fair-procedure requirements for dismissals and said the conflicting rules lose effect within two years.
raw.held: The provision leaving the standard for 'two major demerits' to the Ministry of Civil Service does not fit the constitutional requirement that the conditions be set by law. Related rules must be revised, and the parts that conflict with the ruling lose effect no later than two years after its announcement. Dismissals must follow due legal process and may only be carried out once final.

points.text: The right to serve in public office is protected by Article 18 of the Constitution, and the state must set up systems that also protect civil servants' rights.
Dismissal as a disciplinary penalty restricts the right to hold public office and is in substance a disciplinary sanction, so its conditions must be set by law under Article 23.

The law may authorize an agency to issue supplementary rules, but the purpose, scope and content of the authorization must be specific and clear. The Act did not clearly set the standard for dismissal, leaving it to the Ministry.
When a law uses abstract terms for disciplinary conditions, the meaning must be understandable, foreseeable to those governed, and checkable by courts, under the clarity principle.
Dismissal requires due legal process: a decision by an impartial internal committee, a chance for the person to state their case, and a written decision giving reasons and how to appeal.
Because a dismissed civil servant can bring an administrative appeal, dismissal may only be carried out after it becomes final, though suspension beforehand is allowed.

raw.answer: The case asked whether the Civil Code rule on a married couple's residence (住所) is unconstitutional, because the rule lets one spouse's choice decide if the couple cannot agree. The court found that the rule does not meet the constitutional principles of equality and proportionality. It will lose effect no later than one year after the ruling is announced.
raw.held: Article 1002 of the Civil Code does not meet the constitutional principles of equality and proportionality, and it will lose effect no later than one year after the ruling is announced. The ruling also says that setting a residence is different from the duty to live together, and spouses without a set residence still owe each other that duty.

points.text: Under the article, the husband (or the wife in a marriage where the husband joins the wife's family) ends up with the final say on the residence if the couple refuses to agree or cannot reach agreement, so the law treats people differently by sex and by type of marriage.

People have freedom of residence, meaning the autonomy to choose their own residence, and the rule does not take into account the other spouse's right to choose or the special circumstances of individual cases.

The Civil Code does not require a person to set a residence and does not make the residence the only place where spouses perform the duty to live together, so that duty is not limited to the residence.
Education and job opportunities are now much more equal for men and women, and spouses may work in different places, so a one-sided rule is out of step with current conditions.
Setting a residence differs from the duty to live together, and spouses who have not set a residence must still live together with the aim of a permanent shared life.

who: Husbands who joined the wife's family (贅夫) and their wives

raw.answer: The case asked whether a Ministry of the Interior rule requiring civic groups to put their administrative region's name in their group name is unconstitutional. The court decided that the rule goes beyond what the parent law allows and violates freedom of association, so it loses effect immediately.
raw.held: The rule in point 4 of the Interior Ministry's 'Social Group Permit and Registration Guidelines', which requires groups to use their administrative region's name, exceeds the parent law, infringes freedom of association, and loses effect immediately.

points.text: Freedom of association under Article 14 protects a group's formation, continuation, naming and related activities from unlawful restriction.
A group's name identifies it, shows its nature and purpose, and builds members' identity, so the right to choose and later change its name is protected by freedom of association.
Limits on choosing a group name must meet Article 23's requirements and be set by law or by an order clearly authorized by law.
The People's Organizations Act sets the administrative region as the organizing area but does not say how a group's name must be chosen.
The organizing area serves to fix the supervising authority and the court for registration, not to limit activities, and it is not necessarily linked to the name.
Administrative agencies may only fill in detailed, technical matters and cannot go beyond the parent law, so the region-name rule oversteps and is void.

who: People who form or join such groups
The Ministry of the Interior and other supervising authorities

raw.answer: The case asked whether the University Act and its enforcement rules were unconstitutional in requiring every university to set up a military training office. The court held that this compulsory requirement violates the constitutional protection of university autonomy. The provisions lose effect no later than one year after the ruling is announced.
raw.held: University Act Article 11, paragraph 1, item 6 and Article 9, paragraph 3 of its enforcement rules, which require universities to set up a military training office with staff to plan and teach military training and nursing courses, are unconstitutional. They lose effect no later than one year after the announcement.

points.text: Academic freedom in Article 11 of the Constitution protects university autonomy, covering teaching and learning matters such as course content and students' choice of departments and courses, as the court said in Interpretation No. 380.

Within teaching and research matters, universities should have a fair degree of freedom to organize their own internal structure. Forcing a unit for a course the university does not think it needs conflicts with this.
A university that decides for itself to offer military training or nursing courses may set up related units and hire suitable teachers under the law.
The compulsory military training office rule fails to respect university autonomy, so it is unconstitutional.
Because the ruling affects systems and organization, a transition period of up to one year was allowed before the rules lose effect.

The other required units (academic affairs, student affairs, general affairs, library, secretary, personnel, accounting) do not conflict with university autonomy. The physical education office provision should be reviewed by the relevant authorities.

who: Authorities that make and review university rules

raw.answer: The case asked whether a Supreme Court precedent is unconstitutional. It said a court need not order a person to fix a retrial petition that fails to include evidence that it was filed on time. The Constitutional Court held that the precedent does not conflict with the constitutional protection of the right to bring lawsuits, and that a court may still ask a party to supply the missing evidence in a particular case.
raw.held: The precedent saying no correction needs to be ordered when a retrial petition omits evidence of meeting the fixed time limit is consistent with the constitutional right to sue. Where the petition already states its grounds and evidence for them but omits the timeliness evidence, a court may, depending on the case, order the party to provide it.

points.text: The constitution protects the right to bring lawsuits, including a hearing, fair procedure and equal treatment in procedure.
Retrial is a special remedy that reopens a final judgment, so stricter limits on bringing it are allowed to keep the proceedings fair to both sides and keep final judgments stable.

Evidence of meeting the fixed time limit is a document or item to attach when filing, not part of the form of the petition itself, so it is not something to be corrected. Failing to provide it only affects whether it can be used as a basis for judgment.
The procedure already allows for party autonomy and keeps substantive fairness between the parties, so no correction process is needed.
If what a party states is unclear or incomplete, the presiding judge should use the power to seek clarification and have the party explain or add to it.
The Supreme Court precedent fits these points and therefore does not conflict with the constitutional right to sue.

raw.answer: The case asked whether putting major construction spending into a special budget is unconstitutional, and it also raised disputes over how Article 164 of the Constitution counts the "total budget" for education, science and culture. The court did not rule on whether special budgets for major projects are unconstitutional. It said that, because of a later constitutional amendment, the questions about the "total budget" and the education, science and culture percentages no longer needed interpreting.
raw.held: The court held that the questions about what counts as the "total budget" under Article 164, and the share of budgets going to education, science and culture, need no further interpretation, because the legislature is to decide such matters under the amended Constitution.

points.text: Article 164 sets minimum shares of budgets for education, science and culture, to guarantee stable and necessary public spending in those areas.
Earlier interpretations (Nos. 77 and 231) already held that the "total budget" does not include supplementary or special budgets.

A government should in principle adopt a single budget, but in special emergencies under the Budget Act's listed conditions the Executive Yuan may submit a special budget outside the annual general budget.
If most legislators reviewing a special budget find it does not meet the legal conditions, they may vote to delete it or require the Executive Yuan to redo it.
The amendment of 21 July 1997 says education, science and culture funding gets priority and is not limited by Article 164.
So the amounts, proportions, method of budgeting and scope of those budgets are for the legislature to decide on its own political responsibility, and further interpretation is unnecessary.

who: The Executive Yuan and local governments

raw.answer: The case asked whether Taiwan's Military Service Act rules on who must serve, and on lifting a ban on service, violate the Constitution, including its guarantee of religious freedom. The court decided they do not. It found the duty of men to serve, and the rules for lifting the ban on service, are consistent with equality, religious freedom and proportionality.
raw.held: The rule that men must serve in the military does not conflict with the constitutional guarantees of equality and religious freedom. The rules on lifting the service ban for people given short prison terms, and on re-calling them, also do not conflict with the Constitution.

points.text: The Constitution says people must serve in the military as the law provides, but leaves how to do so to the legislature, which sets key matters by law considering national security and social needs.

Religious freedom protects inner belief absolutely, but religious acts and groups are only relatively protected and remain subject to necessary laws. Religious believers are still citizens and cannot escape basic duties to the state because of faith.

Making men liable for service reflects differences between men and women in biology and social roles. It is a policy choice to serve national purposes, not meant to promote or restrict religion, and it has no such effect.

Military service does not violate human dignity or shake the constitutional value system. Most countries require it and it is necessary to protect people and the nation, so it does not conflict with equality or religious freedom.

A person freed from the service ban after a short actual prison term still owes service if of service age. Punishing a separate violation under the law on obstructing military service is not double punishment and does not breach religious freedom or proportionality.

Calling back to service those whose suspension has ended, and calling them up to complete service time, falls within the Military Service Act's scope for temporary call-ups. It adds no burden on people, so it does not breach the principle that such matters need a legal basis.

who: People who served prison terms and had their service ban lifted
Reservists and those whose service was suspended

raw.answer: The case asked whether a Ministry of Finance letter was unconstitutional. The letter said a building used as a religious altar (神壇) is not a 'residence' for the land tax rules on owner-occupied residential land. The court held that the letter does not violate the Constitution.
raw.held: The Ministry of Finance's 1983 letter, which says a building used as an altar is not a 'residence' under Article 9 of the Land Tax Act, does not conflict with the constitutional principle that taxes must be set by law. It also does not conflict with the equality and religious freedom provisions (Articles 7 and 13).

points.text: Taxpaying and tax exemption must follow written law, but the authorities may explain a law in line with its purpose when its application is unclear. Tax laws are read according to their purpose, economic meaning and fairness.

The Land Tax Act does not define 'residence'. Under the ordinary understanding, a residence is a building fixed to land for daily living, with basic living facilities, controlled by its occupants and highly private.
The letter is a negative interpretation of 'residence' that fits the Act's purpose and stays within the concept of a residence, so it does not breach the principle that taxes be set by law.

Religious land can be relieved of land tax under the Act's rules, whatever the religion. An altar not registered as a legal-person body or temple cannot use the religious-group relief, and that has nothing to do with religious freedom.

An altar is a place where ordinary believers freely set up worship of deities for followers. That differs from the private nature of a residence, so the letter does not impose tax discrimination based on religion.

who: Owners of buildings used as altars
Land owners claiming owner-occupied residence tax rates

raw.answer: The case asked whether a government set of rules on Taiwan entry, long-term residence and household registration was constitutional. Those rules let officials deny or cancel residence permits and household registration for people with no registration in Taiwan, and order them to leave by a deadline. The court held that most of these rules were unconstitutional because they limited residence and movement freedom without a law or clear legal authorization, but it upheld the parts needed to carry out the National Security Act and similar special laws.
raw.held: Most of the rules on denying or cancelling residence and registration, and on ordering people to leave by a deadline, conflict with the Constitution and lose effect no later than one year after the ruling. The parts on unauthorized entry (item 3 of paragraph 1 and the related paragraph 2 provisions) were upheld as needed to carry out special laws such as the National Security Act.

points.text: The Constitution's Article 10 protects freedom to choose where to live, move, and travel, including leaving or entering the country.

Limits on this freedom must meet the necessity standard in Article 23 and be set by law, or by an administrative order under clear authorization from the legislature. Reasonable differences between groups of people are allowed.

The household registration law's authorization covered only registration rules for overseas Chinese, and administrative orders must stay within the authorization's purpose and scope. The Ministry of the Interior also never issued rules under it and sent them to the Legislative Yuan.

Denying entry-based residence or registration to people who entered without permission was upheld, because it is needed to carry out the National Security Act and matches the cross-strait and Hong Kong/Macao relations laws.

The other grounds for denial (suspected security threats, criminal record, forged documents, sham marriage, failed health check, and so on) had no legal or legally authorized basis, yet limited residence and movement by order alone.

The registration and deadline-to-leave provisions applied to all people without registration in Taiwan, except where the cross-strait and Hong Kong/Macao laws provide forced departure, so they also lacked a legal basis. For people from the mainland, Hong Kong and Macao, the relevant laws apply where they exist.

who: People without household registration in Taiwan
Overseas Chinese applying for residence in Taiwan
Residents of Hong Kong and Macao
People who entered Taiwan without permission

raw.answer: The case asked whether the Act for Rebuilding Old Military Dependents' Villages and its rules, which give original village households benefits such as buying new housing, subsidies and low-interest loans, violate the constitution's equality principle. The court decided that the purpose of these benefits does not conflict with equality, but that some provisions are not fully consistent with the principles of limited welfare resources and equality. It told the legislature to review and improve those parts as a whole.
raw.held: The benefits for original households do not conflict with the equality principle in Article 7 of the Constitution. However, the legislature must comprehensively review and improve the parts of the Act that do not match this interpretation.

points.text: Equality under the Constitution means substantive equality, not absolute or mechanical sameness, so reasonable differences in treatment are allowed.
Promoting people's welfare is a basic constitutional principle, and the legislature has wide freedom to distribute limited welfare resources based on social policy and state finances.
Giving original households housing purchase rights, subsidies and low-interest loans aims to help those who need care, so its purpose does not conflict with Article 7.

Because resources are limited, welfare laws must consider the state's finances, equality with ordinary citizens, and beneficiaries' means and need. Special status or position alone cannot be the only basis for different treatment, and benefits must not be clearly excessive.
Defining old villages only by completion date, without considering their actual condition and renewal needs, risks wasting state resources.

Letting children of deceased households receive the same benefits regardless of need is clearly excessive care, and the five-year resale limit alone may not make effective use of subsidized housing, so the legislature should consider tighter limits on resale.

who: Children and spouses of deceased original households

raw.answer: The case asked whether a Ministry of Finance circular was unconstitutional. The circular says a company whose business is trading securities must split its operating expenses and interest between tax-exempt income and taxable income in proportion to revenue. The court held the circular does not conflict with the Constitution, though it said the method should ideally be authorized clearly by statute.
raw.held: The Ministry of Finance's 1994 circular, which splits expenses and interest in proportion to revenue, is consistent with the legal provisions and does not conflict with the Constitution. The court added that how costs and expenses are calculated affects people's tax burden, so it is better for a law to clearly authorize the tax authority to set the rules.

points.text: Under the income tax law, a company's taxable income is its yearly revenue minus costs, expenses, losses and taxes.

Securities trading gains have been exempt from income tax since 1990, and 80% of investment income from certain domestic companies is exempt. By the principle of matching revenue with costs and fairness, the related costs cannot be deducted from other taxable income.
Costs that can be directly and reasonably assigned may be assigned individually and deducted from securities sale revenue.

Investment income and securities trading income come from the same invested cost, so the ratio of invested cost is hard to use as the basis for dividing costs. Using the ratio of revenues is therefore consistent with the law's purpose and does not conflict with the Constitution.
Because calculating costs and expenses affects people's tax burden, Article 19 of the Constitution calls for the law to clearly authorize the tax authority to set such rules.

The claim that applying a 1994 circular to income from 1990 breaks the rule against retroactive application fails. An official interpretation that clarifies a regulation's original meaning applies from the date the regulation took effect, as stated in Interpretation No. 287.

who: Companies whose business is trading securities
Companies holding shares in other domestic companies

raw.answer: The case asked whether a Ministry of the Interior rule barring co-owners from applying to register a ground-use right (superficies) acquired through long-term possession was unconstitutional. The court held that co-owners and joint owners can acquire such a right this way if they meet the requirements. It found the rule inconsistent with the constitutional protection of property and said it should not be applied.
raw.held: The rule in the Ministry of the Interior's 1988 review guidelines, item 3 point 5, which says co-owners may not apply to register a superficies acquired by prescription on co-owned land, violates the constitutional protection of property and is not to be applied.

points.text: Prescription exists for the public good, and property acquired through it is constitutionally protected, as an earlier interpretation (No. 291) had already said.
A superficies is a right to use another's land for buildings, structures or bamboo and trees, and is a kind of usufructuary real right.

A co-owner may use a specific part of co-owned land only with all other co-owners' consent, but the co-owned property can be burdened with the consent of all, so a superficies can be set up for one or several co-owners. The same holds for jointly owned land, where disposing of it requires all joint owners' consent.

Because a superficies is a real right, it can be acquired by prescription, but the possessor must hold the land with the intent to exercise a superficies. Possession that began as a co-owner, as a joint owner, or without right does not qualify unless the intent later changes as the civil code article 945 provides.
A co-owner or joint owner who tells the others they now possess the land with the intent to exercise a superficies can claim it by prescription and ask to be registered as the holder.
So the rule banning co-owners from applying is inconsistent with this and violates the constitutional protection of property.

who: Other co-owners or joint owners who allowed the possession

raw.answer: The case challenged a rule of the Veterans Affairs Commission on what happens to farm land and housing after a veteran farm worker dies. The rule let a son inherit the right to keep using the land and housing, but required a daughter to give them up once she married. The court found this unequal treatment of women contrary to the gender equality principle and told the authority to review the rule.
raw.held: The rule's provision that lets only a veteran's son, married or not, inherit the right to the land and housing, while daughters must return them after marriage, does not fit the gender equality principle. The authority must review the relevant rules and handle the matter properly within six months of the ruling's publication.

points.text: The Constitution says all people are equal before the law regardless of sex, and the state must promote substantive equality between the sexes. State organs must follow this even when they use private-law acts to carry out public tasks.
Farm land allocated to veterans was a special benefit, different from rights ordinary citizens get. The veteran and the state formed a free-of-charge loan-for-use relationship.
When the veteran died or the loan's purpose ended, the authority should normally end the arrangement and take back the land so state resources are used sensibly.

If the authority chooses to let surviving family keep using the land and housing, it must consider whether children are included and whether they need continued support given their ability to earn a living and farm, and plan according to gender equality so people in the same legal position get equal care.
The rule favored sons regardless of their ability to support themselves or any need for help, and regardless of marriage. Daughters had to give up the land when they married.
Whether farm land allocation can be inherited at all was set aside, but treating certain women differently just because of sex and marital status violates gender equality.

who: Daughters of deceased veteran farm workers
Sons of deceased veteran farm workers

raw.answer: The case asked whether a rule in the Trademark Act is unconstitutional. The rule bars registering a trademark design that contains another group's name without that group's consent. The court decided the rule does not conflict with the Constitution, because it protects such groups' names and also protects consumers.
raw.held: The court held that the Trademark Act provision barring registration of a trademark design containing another group's name without its consent does not conflict with Article 22 of the Constitution. It also held that certain groups without legal personality can be protected under the trademark law and the Constitution.
